en: The Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Instruction to King Prasenajit, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
At the Jetavana Monastery, [the Buddha] was together with a vast assembly of immeasurable bhikṣus, devas, and others.

At that time, the Great King Prasenajit, Lord of Kośala, who had fully accomplished both noble rank and majestic virtue, prepared his carriage and departed from the city to go to the place where the Tathāgata was, desiring to behold and question the Buddha.

Having traveled by carriage to the lower area, he proceeded on foot into the garden. From afar, he saw the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree, majestic and sublime; his faculties were serene and his mind was tranquil. He had already attained the supreme, perfectly disciplined, and ultimate state of calm abiding; he had already reached the foremost shore of perfect discipline and tranquility. He skillfully guarded and subdued his sense-faculties, acting as a dragon among men, a bull-king among men, and a noble steed among men. Pure and undisturbed, he was like a clear spring or pool; his majestic virtue was blazing and his radiance shone forth like a great mountain of gold. He was fully adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his limbs embellished by the eighty secondary characteristics.

At that time, King Jayasena, having seen the Buddha from afar, was so overcome with joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately removed all five of the royal insignia and ornaments belonging to a consecrated Great King of the Kṣatriya caste:
first, the jeweled crown upon his head; second, the divine sword he held; [third, the royal parasol; fourth, the fly-whisk; fifth, the golden slippers].
Third, canopies made of various jewels;
fourth, fans and fly-whisks made of mani-jewels;
fifth, woven jewel slippers.

Having departed from there, he went to the place where the Tathāgata was. Upon arrival, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, after King Jayasena had sat down at one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!

I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately instruct me; I only pray that the Sugata will compassionately admonish me, so that I may realize great meaning, benefit, and happiness throughout the long night.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Great King:
"Excellent, excellent, Great King!"
It is well that you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a great meaning. Great King!

As you are now the sovereign of a great kingdom, you should employ the True Dharma and not the false dharma; you should act in accordance with the Dharma and not in accordance with what is contrary to the Dharma.
Why is this so? "Great King, you should know!

If there are kings or other rulers who abandon the True Dharma and act as kings through various false dharmas, they will be reviled by the noble ones in the present life; later, they will fall into grief and regret, and when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will fall into the evil destinies, being born in the hells to undergo various intense sufferings."

Furthermore, if a king or various rulers abandon false teachings and govern as kings by means of the True Dharma, they will be praised by the multitude of noble sages in the present life; later, free from sorrow or regret, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will ascend to a happy destination and be born among the devas to experience sublime pleasures.
“Great King! Just as parents feel compassion for their children and always desire in their hearts that they be free from suffering and attain happiness,

so too should you act toward all sentient beings in every kingdom and town— whether they be servants, laborers, ministers, or officials— and bestow upon them the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) taught by the Buddhas.”
What are the four? First, giving; second, kind speech;
Third is beneficial conduct;
fourth is cooperation.

In this way, one skillfully gathers the sentient beings of the country and its towns, as well as servants, laborers, ministers, and officials, bringing them together through these two purposes so that they share the same work and return to the same goal.
What are these two meanings? First, the present; second, the future.
"Great King, you should know this!

For example, suppose a man or a woman, within a dream, perceives with their dreaming mind lovely gardens, lovely mountains and valleys, lovely cities and towns, along with various other things; yet once they have awakened from that dream, none of what was seen remains."
Thus it is, Great King!
Sovereignty, life, and the body are false and impermanent; all are like what is seen in a dream.
"Great King, you should know this!"

The pleasures of royal wealth and status, the pleasures of royal sovereignty, the pleasures of royal desire, and all other implements for enjoying sensual pleasures—namely, the elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry divisions; palaces; queens, crown princes, and various kings; ministers, officials, and guards; parents, brothers, sisters, wives, and concubines; men, women, children, servants, laborers, and the inhabitants of the realm; gold, silver, precious gems, pearls, clothing, wealth, grain, and storehouses—all such implements for sensual enjoyment must be abandoned at the time of death. One departs alone for the next world, with not a single thing to follow.

"Great King, you should know that all these aforementioned articles of pleasure are impermanent, non-eternal, and unreliable. They are all subject to change, fleeting and unceasing; they circulate and shift until they ultimately meet with destruction. Moment by moment they pass away and later become ashes; in the end, they all converge upon the gate of extinction. These are phenomena of loss and ruin, fraught with terrors and calamities, and abounding in sorrow and affliction; they are all phenomena of falling, withering, severance, and dispersal."
"Great King, you should know this!

It is like a forest where one first sees the flowers in bloom, which are soon followed by fruit, only for the fruit later to vanish; or where one first sees the leaves flourishing and lush green, which soon turn withered and yellow, until finally they all fall away."
In this way, Great King!

Your royal dominion, your life, your kingly wealth and pleasures, your kingly sovereignty and pleasures, your kingly sensual pleasures, and all other cherished objects of desire—namely, the elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry forces, and so forth, as explained at length—are likewise subject to falling, withering, breaking, and dispersal. It is exactly thus.
"Great King, you should know this!

It is like a great mass of fire: first it is seen blazing, then it blazes intensely, then it blazes all-pervasively, and finally it becomes completely incandescent; though it burns fiercely for a long time, it ultimately returns to total extinction."
In this way, Great King!

The sovereignty of the kingdom, one's life, the pleasures of royal wealth and status, the pleasures of royal sovereignty, the pleasures of royal desire, and all other instruments for enjoying sensual pleasures—namely, the elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry forces, and so forth in detail—all are likewise subject to the nature of falling, decaying, breaking apart, and dispersing. Thus it is.

"Great King, you should know that just as the orbs of the sun and moon possess great divine attributes and immense power, emitting vast radiance to adorn themselves and illuminating the entire world, they ultimately fade away and disappear."
In this same way, Great King!

Your royal lineage, your life, your royal wealth and pleasures, your royal pleasures of sovereignty, your royal pleasures of sensual desire, and all other instruments of enjoyment—namely, the elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry divisions, and so forth in detail—all are likewise subject to the nature of falling, decaying, breaking apart, and dispersing.
“Great King, you should know!

It is like a great cloud that covers the entirety of space; with violent winds, swift thunder, flashing lightning, and pouring rain, it shakes heaven and earth only to vanish and be extinguished in an instant.”
In this same way, Great King!

Your royal lineage, your life, the pleasures of royal wealth and status, the pleasures of royal sovereignty, the pleasures of royal desire, and all other instruments of sensual enjoyment you possess—namely, the elephant, cavalry, chariot, and infantry forces, and so forth in detail—are likewise subject to the nature of falling, withering, breaking, and dispersing. It is just like this.

Therefore, Great King, you should cultivate diligent practice, contemplating impermanence and contemplating exhaustion and cessation. You should always remain apprehensive regarding the end of your own life; as a great king, you should act according to the True Dharma and not according to what is contrary to the Dharma, following the path of the Dharma and not following what is contrary to the Dharma.
"Great King, you should know this!

Suppose four great mountains were to come from the four directions—solid, firm, dense, without gaps or interstices, completely filling the space and merging into one whole, reaching from the very summit of space down to the limits of the earth. Within them, all grasses, trees, branches, twigs, flowers, and leaves, as well as all sentient beings and crawling creatures, would be ground to dust. It would be difficult to escape by means of swift valor, difficult to resist through physical strength, and difficult to ward off by means of incantations, wealth, or medicinal herbs."
Thus it is, Great King!

There are four kinds of great terrors in the world, each coming to grind and destroy all sentient beings; they are difficult to escape by means of resolute courage, difficult to resist by means of power or force, and difficult to prohibit by means of incantations, wealth, or medicinal herbs.
“What are the four kinds of great terrors?
Great King, you should know:
first, the arrival of old age comes to oppress and harm, grinding away the youth and vigor of sentient beings.”
Second, illness comes as an affliction, destroying the well-being of sentient beings;
third, death comes as an affliction, destroying the life-span of sentient beings;
fourth, decline comes as an affliction, destroying the prosperity of sentient beings.
"Great King, you should know!
It is like a lion, the king of beasts, who enters a herd of deer and seizes one; whether it has already eaten or not yet eaten, he does so with complete ease and without hindrance."
At that time, the deer, though previously so full of vigor and courage, could do nothing once it had entered the lion’s mouth.
In the same way, Great King,
once all sentient beings have entered the mouth of the lion-king of impermanence, all their power and strength can no longer avail them.
"Great King, you should know this!
For example, suppose there is a person who is brave and possesses great strength; yet, once struck by a poisoned arrow, all his prowess is utterly destroyed.
In the same way, Great King!"

All sentient beings are stubborn and perverse; when struck by the arrow of death, they possess no further strength, no further protection, no refuge, and nowhere to flee. As they approach the end of life and their limbs are severed, their flesh and blood dry up and their hearts burn with affliction. Driven by parching thirst, they gasp with gaping mouths; their hands and feet are in disarray and they lack all capability. Devoid of power, saliva and mucus flow together, while urine and excrement defile their bodies. The six sense-faculties are blocked, the throat and palate are constricted, and their labored breathing becomes ever more urgent, as even a skilled physician stands with folded hands, setting aside all his wondrous medicines.

All the exquisite flavors and precious delicacies they have consumed are entirely abandoned; as they lie prostrate upon their beds and pillows, on the verge of departing for another realm and sinking into the boundless depths, they are swept away by the torrential flood of impermanence—birth, old age, sickness, and death. Reaching the stage of the end of life, with but little remaining vitality, it is through the power of karma that the next existence manifests before them.

Terrified by the messengers of King Yama, swallowed by the vast darkness of the night, with the final exhalation and inhalation about to cease, one stands alone without a second or any companion, suddenly turning one's back on this life to return to the next world.

This is a great transition toward a vast forest, entering great darkness and wandering through a great wilderness; drifting upon the great ocean, tossed by the winds of karma, one goes toward a direction that is signless and profound obscurity. At such a time, there is no other protection, no other refuge, and no other place of retreat, except for the True Dharma alone.
"Great King!

At that time, only the True Dharma can provide protection, can serve as a palace, and can act as a refuge; it is that toward which one must hasten and that into which one must flee, for it can uproot sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death."
"Great King, you should know this!
For example, if a person is oppressed by the suffering of cold, only warm fire, sunlight, clothing, and the like can bring it to an end and allow them to find peace;
if they are oppressed by the suffering of heat, only forests, springs, and the like [can do so]."
If one travels a long distance, there is only the cool shade;
if oppressed by thirst, only pure, cool water;
if oppressed by hunger, only abundant and delicious food; and if oppressed by illness, only a skilled physician, medicine, and an attendant.
If one is oppressed by fear, one seeks only a powerful companion.

In the same way, Great King, when all beings are struck by the arrow of death, they have no further power, no further protection, no refuge, and no place to flee. As they approach the end of life and their limbs are severed, their flesh and blood dry up and their hearts are tormented by fever; driven by parching thirst, they gasp with open mouths, their hands and feet flailing in confusion until they are rendered powerless. To speak at length, at that time, for them there is only the True Dharma (*saddharma*) that can provide protection, serve as a palace, and act as a refuge. It is that toward which they must rush and that into which they must flee; it is able to pull sentient beings out from the suffering of birth and death.
Why is this so? "Great King, you should know that such a body,

though guarded and protected, though long washed and adorned, and though satiated with a multitude of the most excellent and refined foods at its will, nevertheless, when the time of death arrives, cannot escape the oppression of hunger and thirst, and thus must relinquish its life."
"Great King, you should know this:

although such a body is constantly bathed and adorned at will with unguents, powdered incense, burning incense, and flower garlands, because its very substance is composed of foul secretions, at the time of death it will inevitably return to impurity and stench."
"Great King, you should know this:

although such a body is covered and wrapped with various kinds of exquisite garments, because it is composed of various impure substances, at the time of death, these various impurities must inevitably flow forth."
"Great King, you should know this:

although such a body may dwell in a palace surrounded by queens, concubines, court ladies, beauties, and retinues, enjoying itself with various musical performances and diverse entertainments in joy and happiness, at the time of death it will see its own evil omens and will inevitably be struck with terror, grief, sorrow, and anguish."
"Great King, you should know this:
although such a body may dwell within palace chambers, adorned with colorful paintings, in halls, pavilions, and towers, with doors, windows,
and balconies tightly shut behind multiple locks, and though it is embellished with various fragrant flowers and various lamps and candles— "
Increasing the radiance and illumination, they arranged rare and wondrous screens and canopies; they burned various famous incenses and scattered all manner of exquisite flowers.

Incense burners, flower vases, and jeweled jars were displayed everywhere, and various couches and seats made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and other precious gems were set out, covered with superior and wonderful woolen rugs, brocades, embroidered mats, and floral carpets. Upon these couches and seats—
At both ends are placed vermilion pillows, covered with exquisite silk cloths and brocade quilts;
while awake or asleep, they rest in peace, indulging in pleasure and attachment. Yet after the end of life, they have no further perception or awareness.
Their corpses may be sent to a burial site, where crows, magpies, eagles, vultures, foxes, wolves, jackals, hungry dogs, owls, and various other malevolent birds and beasts [devour them].

They scramble together to eat and consume [the corpse], its flesh, bones, pus, blood, hair, and beard, along with its excrement and filth, overflowing upon the ground in a place so foul as to be loathsome.
"Great King, you should know this!

Such a person as this formerly constantly rode upon fragrant elephants, swift horses, and various precious litters and carriages; drums were beaten and conchs blown to produce great music, while canopies of many jewels followed in attendance behind. Fans and fly-whisks were held aloft to provide shade and movement, while immeasurable, valiant armies of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry escorted them before and after. Hundreds of thousands of ministers and officials guarded them on the left and right, serving with utmost sincerity and devotion, while the citizens and commoners of the cities and towns joined their palms in awe and admiration.

Although one may enjoy such supreme and wondrous karmic rewards—sovereignty, glory, and splendor—for long, one must before long close one's eyes and withdraw one's hands, no longer moving; the corpse will lie prostrate upon the funeral bier, borne out through the great city gate by a multitude of people. Parents, wives, children, brothers, sisters, servants, laborers, officials, and aides, along with kinsmen and female attendants following on either side, their hearts bound by grief and distress, their hair disheveled, raise their hands to strike their heads and beat their breasts in choked sobs. Overwhelmed by sorrow and collapsing in lamentation, they all cry out:
"Alas! How bitter!"
The people of the cities and towns beheld this and were filled with longing and grief. They followed him to the place of burial;

some left the body exposed as an offering for birds and beasts—crows, magpies, hungry dogs, vultures, eagles, owls, hawks, foxes, wolves, jackals, and various predatory beasts—which tore at and devoured the flesh and bones until they were scattered in disarray. Exposed to the wind, scorched by the sun, drenched by rain, and encased in frost, the limbs and joints fell apart and were dispersed in different places.

Others piled up firewood to cremate the body; the tendons and bones were charred and rotted, the flesh and blood were consumed, and foul smoke billowed forth, filling the four directions. When the fire was extinguished and the bones had vanished, the ashes flew away and the dust dissipated.
Or there are those who dig into the earth to bury their remains in graves and mounds, where over the passage of much time the flesh decays and the bones rot.

"Great King, you should know that this body is thus subject to transformation and destruction, impermanent. All sentient beings and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are exactly like this: they are neither eternal nor constant, and cannot be relied upon. They are all phenomena of change, shifting without ceasing; they flow and move until they ultimately return to ruin and extinction. Moment by moment they pass away and become ashes; in the end, they all tend toward the gate of total cessation. These are phenomena of loss and decay, fraught with terrors and calamities, abounding in sorrows and afflictions—all are phenomena of falling, withering, severing, breaking, and dispersal."

"Therefore, Great King, you should diligently cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and the contemplation of exhaustion and cessation. Do not be defiled by greed, do not be agitated by hatred, and do not be obscured by delusion. Do not again become addicted to the pleasures of royal wealth and status; do not again become addicted to the pleasures of royal sovereignty; do not again become addicted to the pleasures of royal sensual desire; and do not again become addicted to any other objects of sensory enjoyment."

You should eliminate pride and negligence regarding wealth and life; you should be struck with awe and fear toward the Māra of impermanence and death, which arrives suddenly without appointment with anyone.

As a great sovereign of a nation, you should employ the True Dharma and not the unrighteous; you should follow the practice of the Dharma and not that which is contrary to it; you should pity all sentient beings as if they were your only child; and you should sincerely protect and uphold the Buddha-Dharma, ensuring the prosperity of the Triple Gem without looking elsewhere.

Why is this so? Wandering through the ocean of birth and death has been without beginning; only the True Dharma of the Buddha serves as the great bridge and ferry, for it is truly difficult to encounter even in the course of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
"Great King, you should know this!

I do not say that one who acquires and enjoys the various worldly objects of sensual pleasure and amasses them is called 'wealthy and noble. I say that one who acquires and enjoys the treasure of the noble wisdom of the True Dharma of all Buddhas and amasses it is truly called one who has attained perfect wealth and nobility."
Therefore, Great King,
you should cultivate weary detachment toward all the worldly requisites for sensual pleasure, and you should aspire to seek the noble wisdom-treasures of the True Dharma of the Buddhas.

When the Blessed One had spoken this sutra, the Great King Prasenajit, Lord of Kośala, along with the assembly of devas, humans, and others in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Instruction to King Jayasena.
